papers.title: A large EEG dataset for studying cross-session variability in motor imagery brain-computer interface.
papers.key_finding: In a dataset of 25 participants across five days, within-session classification accuracy was reported as up to 68.8%, cross-session accuracy was 53.7%, and cross-session adaptation accuracy was 78.9%.
papers.limitation: The reported results are dataset benchmarks across five recording days; they do not test sustained home use, assistive performance, or rehabilitation outcomes.
papers.neuroweave_relevance: Supports session-associated decoding performance changes and motivates testing adaptation, but does not identify the cause of the changes.

papers.title: Discrepancy between inter- and intra-subject variability in EEG-based motor imagery brain-computer interface: Evidence from multiple perspectives.
papers.key_finding: The study reports that variability can reduce model generalization and that cross-session and cross-subject EEG feature patterns differ, suggesting they may require different training-sample selection strategies.
papers.limitation: The study does not establish the mechanism causing session changes or test everyday assistive use.
papers.neuroweave_relevance: Contextualizes session variability as distinct from between-person variability and cautions against inferring a specific cause from performance changes alone.

papers.title: Session-independent subject-adaptive mental imagery BCI using selective filter-bank adaptive Riemannian features.
papers.key_finding: The proposed features showed around 15% and 8% improvement in mean accuracy over baseline and fixed filter-bank models, respectively, across four public datasets.
papers.limitation: The study covers mental imagery beyond motor imagery and reports dataset-based evaluation rather than everyday home-use or rehabilitation outcomes.
papers.neuroweave_relevance: Supports the relevance of inter-session variation as a robustness challenge and reports an adaptive approach, but does not establish real-world reliability or the cause of drift.

papers.title: Improving inter-session performance via relevant session-transfer for multi-session motor imagery classification.
papers.key_finding: Relevant-session transfer improved performance by 2.29% on the Shu dataset (p < 0.001) and by up to 6.37% on the authors' gait-related motor-imagery dataset, compared with self-calibration.
papers.limitation: The evaluation used two datasets and does not report a home-use trial, sustained deployment, or clinical benefit.
papers.neuroweave_relevance: Directly supports cross-session performance change and reports a transfer-based mitigation approach, but does not identify why session data differ.

papers.title: Unsupervised Domain Adaptation With Synchronized Self-Training for Cross-Domain Motor Imagery Recognition.
papers.key_finding: The proposed synchronized self-training domain-adaptation method outperformed comparison methods in inter-session experiments, using labeled source-domain data and unlabeled target-domain data.
papers.limitation: The abstract reports evaluation on public datasets and a new six-class dataset, but does not report home-use or clinical-outcome testing.
papers.neuroweave_relevance: Supports the practical importance of distribution changes across domains and sessions and the potential value of adaptation, but does not establish the underlying cause of those changes.
